title: The Wanderer and the Earth
hookLine: a king meets a young wanderer with nothing, and asks where his calm comes from
carry: the earth is a guru: pushed, it doesn't swerve
tomorrow: who is the path of action really for?

lines: WHERE DOES YOUR CALM COME FROM?
cards: A king out in the world meets a young man who owns nothing. No house, no plans, no worry on his face. The king is Yadu, an ancestor of Krishna's own clan, and he can't help asking.
You're clever and capable, he says, yet you live like a child, untroubled. People all around are burning with wanting, and you stand there cool, like an elephant in a river while the forest burns.
Where does your calm come from? Krishna tells this story to Uddhava early in their dialogue. The wanderer is an avadhuta, one who lives outside the world's usual rules.
His answer: I've had many teachers. And the first one is right under your feet.

teach.h: THE EARTH: PUSHED, AND STILL STEADY.
teach.b: The first teacher is the earth.

teach.h: OTHERS ARE MOVED BY CAUSES TOO.
teach.b: In paraphrase, here's what the avadhuta learned from it: a steady person, even when pushed around by other beings, remembers that they too are moved by forces beyond their control, and doesn't step off the path.
People dig the earth, plow it, build on it and walk on it all day. It doesn't shake anyone off. It keeps holding things up and growing food.
This is karma from an unexpected side. Karma talk often starts with my actions and what comes back to me. The avadhuta turns it around.
The other person, the one acting badly, is caught in a web of causes too. Not excused. Understood.
Their action is theirs; my steadiness is mine. And the earth doesn't pretend nothing happened, or argue.

teach.h: NOT A DOORMAT: JUST DON'T SWERVE.
teach.b: It simply doesn't swerve. That isn't being a doormat. It's not letting someone else's bad day rewrite your path.
After the earth come twenty-three more: the wind, the sky, water, fire, the moon, a python, a moth, a honeybee and others.

Tradition identifies the wanderer with Dattatreya, and many Hindus know this list as his twenty-four gurus. That's the teaching: in Hinduism, a guru can be anything you learn from, and the world itself is a classroom.
The list begins at the ground, with the teacher everybody stands on.

how: The avadhuta's list of teachers in the Bhagavata's eleventh book is a familiar teaching story among Hindus, and tradition identifies the avadhuta with Dattatreya, honored as a teacher of teachers.

o: action, and the web of causes that moves it
a mantra you chant at every sunrise for luck
a fixed fate written at your birth

s: the avadhuta names the earth as one of his teachers
the earth comes first of twenty-four: pushed around, it stays steady and doesn't swerve.
the earth's lesson is to let anyone walk all over you
it's not to step off your own path, while seeing that others are moved by causes too.
Krishna tells the avadhuta's story to Uddhava
Krishna retells the meeting between King Yadu and the wanderer inside his teaching.

games.q: you're the avadhuta. people push you around and treat you badly. what did the earth teach you to do?
o: see that they're moved by causes too, and keep to your path.
move somewhere nobody can reach you.
games.why: the earth's lesson: others are moved by forces beyond their control, so the steady person doesn't swerve. no revenge, no running.

practice: Feel what's holding you up, the chair, the floor, the earth under the building, and let your weight go into it.

Bring to mind one person who pushed you lately with a sharp word or a careless move, and without replaying it, say to yourself: they were moved by things I can't see; then come back to the ground holding you.
If you pray, you can hold that person before the One you pray to.

wordCard.voice: Karma. Action, and the web of causes behind it. From the earth the avadhuta learned that others are moved by causes too, and not to swerve.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a wanderer free of the world's usual rules; the young teacher in Krishna's story.

carryVoice: Your line: the earth is a guru, pushed, it doesn't swerve. The ground takes every step and still holds. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 11.7.24–35 (Krishna tells of King Yadu meeting the young avadhuta; Yadu's question; the list of twenty-four teachers)
Bhagavata Purana 11.7.37 (the lesson of the earth: harassed by beings who act under forces beyond them, the wise do not swerve)
